blocks.p: Dr. Imre Lucan was the first man Sol had ever seen wear glass on his face.

Two small ovals in a wire frame sat halfway down a long thin nose, and the doctor looked over them when Sol came in and through them when he went back to what he was writing. He did not get up. He was lean, with close-cropped grey hair and a lined, narrow face, and he wrote with a pen, in a bound book, in a small upright hand, and he finished his sentence before he spoke.
“Sit,” he said. “Lyda tells me you’re four hundred and some years old and have recently become interesting.”

The surgery was one long room above a chandlery on the main boardwalk. It smelled of soap and spirit and damp paper. Rain ran down the window at the far end. Along one wall there were shelves of printed books, their spines swollen with the river air, and in the corner, under a dust sheet, stood a shape Sol knew at once: a diagnostic couch of the church’s pattern, the same make he had seen in every infirmary from Abundance to Serenity.
“Does it work?”

“When the parts come and the uplink holds and the sun isn’t in a temper.” Lucan capped his pen. “Our sun throws off a flare every few days, and for an hour afterward every Halo on this river reads as noise, and the couch tells me my patients are all infected at once. On a good day it reads half of them as noise anyway.” He pulled the sheet off. “For the sake of form.”
Sol lay down. The hood above his head hummed and warmed, and he felt the old faint prickle at his temple as the machine reached for the coin under his skin.
The console said: No signal.
Lucan looked at it a moment, then turned it off and put the sheet back. “That’s the most honest it’s been in years. Come and sit where I can see you.”

He examined Sol with his hands, the way Sol had once watched a jeweler in Abundance examine a stone, as if nothing else in the room existed. He shone a small light into each eye. He had Sol follow his finger and squeeze his hands, struck below each knee with a little rubber hammer, listened through a tube to his heart.
“Tongue out. To the left.”
Sol did. Lucan bent and looked.
“You bit the side. It’s nearly healed. People who faint don’t bite the side of the tongue.” He sat back. “Tell me about the first time. Not the big one. The first time anything was wrong.”

So Sol told him: the thumb behind his left eye, and the minutes it took with it. The window in Concord. The corridor on Serenity. The transit platform in Abundance with a quarter of an hour gone. Lucan wrote, and now and then asked a question in a dry, level voice, precise as a blade. Always the left? Did anyone see you during the lost time? What were you doing with your hands?
“I don’t know. I don’t remember any of it.”
“No. You wouldn’t. Now the big one.”
Sol told him about the packet, and unbuckling his harness, and stopped.
“Go on.”
“It will sound foolish.”
“Most things do, said aloud in this room.”

“I smelled rain,” Sol said. “Rain on hot stone, on a packet in space. And something rose in me, here.” He touched his stomach, then his chest. “As if the floor of me had come loose. And the light got very bright.”

Lucan had stopped writing. Something had come into his face that had not been there before. It was not surprise. It was the look of a man who has been reading about a country for thirty years and has just met someone who has been there.
“Rain is common,” he said quietly. “So is smoke. Burnt things. Sometimes flowers. And the rising, from the stomach to the throat. Then the light, or a sound, or nothing. Then the fall.”

He went to a cabinet and brought out a flat wooden case with a row of dials along its front and a drum of paper across its top, and beneath the drum a line of thin metal arms, each ending in a pen. A bundle of wires came out of the back, each ending in a small cup.

“This is older than the church,” he said. “Older than Renewal. I built it from a drawing in a book, over about four years, out of parts the chandler downstairs was glad to be rid of. It doesn’t need an uplink. It doesn’t need anything from anyone.”

He parted Sol’s hair with a comb and pressed the cups to his scalp one by one with a dab of cold paste, measuring between them with a tape, until wires ran from Sol’s head to the box like the strings of an instrument. Then he touched a switch. The drum turned. The pens began to move, scratching small restless lines across the rolling paper, and Sol understood after a moment that he was watching himself. All his remembered life a coin in his temple had read every thought he had and carried it away to Sion, and he had never seen a line of it. Here it was, written out in ink in a room above a chandlery, as plain as a ship’s log.
“Breathe fast,” Lucan said. “Deep and fast, until I tell you.”
Sol breathed. His fingers began to tingle. Lucan held a lamp close to his face and flicked it on and off, quick and steady, and the light beat against his closed eyelids in a white pulse.
The pressure came behind his left eye. Only a touch, a thumb laid against the inside of the bone and lifted.

The pens jumped. He heard it: a small sharp scratch out of rhythm with the rest, and then another. Lucan stopped the drum and tore off the strip and laid it flat under his hand, and with a pencil from behind his ear drew a small neat circle on the paper, and then a second. In the third line from the top, among the small grey waves, the ink had gone sharp and tall, two spikes like the teeth of a saw.
“There,” Lucan said. “That’s your thumb.”
He took off his glasses and rubbed the bridge of his nose.

“Left side, a little deep. There’s a fold of the brain there that keeps smell and memory very close together. When it misfires, people smell what isn’t in the room. They feel the rising. They lose time. If the storm spreads across the whole brain at once, they cry out and fall and shake.” He put the glasses back on. “The church calls it the Virus. It isn’t one, and nobody catches it. It’s an illness of the brain, as old as brains. It has a name. It’s called epilepsy.”
Sol said the word to himself. It had a strange shape in the mouth.

“From the Greek, for being seized. Taken hold of. The ancients called it the sacred disease, because a man in a fit looks like a man a god has got hold of.” Lucan reached to the shelf without looking and came back with a fat swollen volume open at a ribbon. “There’s a physician in here, older than nearly anything, who thought that was nonsense. It seems to me no more divine or sacred than any other disease, but has a natural cause. Men call it divine because they do not understand it.” He closed the book. “I’ve agreed with him for thirty-one years.”
“And now?”
Lucan did not answer at once. He began to take the cups off Sol’s scalp, wiping each with a cloth.
“In thirty-one years on this river I’ve seen it eleven times that I know of,” he said. “People hide it. I’m required to report every case to the chapel. I’ve reported none.”
“Why not?”

“Because of what they say afterward.” His hands kept moving. “Every one of them. A fisherman’s wife who couldn’t read a cargo slip lay on the floor of a fish shed and said, as clearly as I’m talking to you, Be still, and know. Know what? She didn’t remember saying it. A boy off a barge told me about a light shining in the dark. An old woman said a word I’d never heard in my life, and wept, and asked me who it was.” He set the last cup in the box. “A disease doesn’t usually have a vocabulary. The fit is ordinary. What comes after it isn’t.”
Sol put his shirt back on. His fingers fumbled at the fastenings.
“Something spoke to me,” he said. “On the packet, in the light. Before I fell.”
“They often do. Usually it’s their mother.”
“It asked me why I was hunting it. I asked who it was. It said, Seek Christ, and you will find me.”

He said the name aloud in the surgery in an ordinary voice, and the rain went on against the window. Lucan did not flinch. He did not touch his temple or glance at the door. He sat very still, and then he picked up his pen and wrote, and Sol saw the shape of the word go down on the page.

“That’s it,” Lucan said. “The old woman’s word.” He looked at it on the page awhile. “There are old drugs, from before Renewal. I can make one or two of them in the back room, with patience. They would quiet it. They might stop it. They would quiet a few other things as well.”
“Would they stop the voice?”
“I have no idea. I don’t know what the voice is.”
Sol thought of the white light, which had seen all the way through him and held him anyway, and of the quiet that had come after the hum stopped, which did not press and did not ask.
“Then not yet,” he said.
Lucan wrote: Declines treatment. He underlined it once.
“Lyda says you went blind.”
“For three days. A dockworker put his hands over my eyes and prayed. Something came away from them, like ash. Then I could see.”
Lucan looked at him a long moment over the glasses. Then he wrote, and Sol read it upside down: Sight recovered, third day. Mechanism unknown. He underlined unknown twice.
“When did you go dark?”
“Ten days ago.”
“Come to the window.”

He turned Sol’s face to the copper light with two cool fingers under the jaw. He parted the hair above Sol’s ears and looked closer. He pinched the skin on the back of Sol’s hand and watched it settle. Then he wrote for some time.
“Grey above both ears, more on the left. Fine lines at the outer corners of the eyes. Were those there a month ago?”
“I don’t know.”
Lucan held out a small round mirror.

Sol had seen his face every morning of his life. It looked back at him now, and it was his face. And beside his left eye there was a line he had never seen, fine as a hair, running out toward the temple like a crack in glaze. Above his ear, where Tobin had found the first white hair, there were others. Not many. Enough that the dark there had gone faintly dull, like metal left out in the rain.
He gave the mirror back.

“Jory Hask went dark four years ago,” Lucan said. “The chapel calls it a fault in his Halo. I watched him put on a year a month, near enough, for most of a year. Then it slowed, and now he’s simply old, the ordinary way. But Jory had only been renewed a handful of times, and he isn’t a talker.” He put the mirror away. “You’ve been renewed for four hundred years. Whatever is coming for you is coming from a long way off.”
He turned the strip from the drum round on the table so that Sol could see it.
“It isn’t a fault. Look here. Not at the spikes. Lower.”

The bottom two lines came from the cups in front of each ear. Under their small grey waves ran a second thing: a fine fast tremor in the ink, uneven, like the line a hand makes writing in a moving cart.

“I didn’t circle that,” Lucan said, “because it isn’t your fits. They come and go. That doesn’t. I’ve had half this river on that drum, and I’ve seen it in six people. Seven, now. Jory was the first. Every one of them came to me dark, and not one of the six has ever had a fit in his life.”
“Where does it come from?”

“Deep. I put a fine wire in under Jory’s cheekbone, the old way, to get nearer, and it was loudest in the amygdala.” He saw Sol’s face. “The almond. There’s one each side, deep in the temple. It does fear, mostly. It sits next door to the fold your fits start in. I don’t know what to make of that, so I’ve written it down and left it alone.”

He tapped the strip. “A Halo doesn’t read a mind the way you read a page. It has to find you first. There’s a rhythm your brain keeps under everything else, as particular to you as your voice, and the Halo locks on to it and rides it, the way a voice on the relay rides its carrier. Everything goes in and out on that lock: the reading, the backup, whatever the hood writes at Renewal. The chapel calls it tuning. It’s in their service manual, which they send out with the parts and assume nobody reads.”
“And this?”

“This is ragged where it starts. But it pulls everything near it into a rhythm of its own, the way a crowd falls into step, and that rhythm sits a hair off the Halo’s carrier, and louder. Two notes that close beat against each other, like two strings a hair out of tune. It crowds the carrier. The Halo hunts for you underneath it and can’t hold you. It can’t read you, so there’s nothing to back up. It can’t write to you, because writing goes in by the same door. As far as the Halo can tell, the man it was tuned to isn’t there anymore.”
Sol said nothing.

“The coin still knows where it is, and the pulse still carries you through a crossing; neither needs to know who you are. But the six all told me, first thing, that the hum stopped. I’d always taken the hum for the sound of the coin. I think it’s the lock. You hear it holding on to you. When it can’t, it stops.”

“The chapel calls this noise,” Lucan said. “So does the couch. A flare drowns the Halos from outside, and passes. This comes from inside, and doesn’t. Noise is only what you call a signal you can’t read.”
“Then what is it?”

“I don’t know what it is. I know what it does to the signal.” He let the strip curl back on itself. “It isn’t the river. I had a man on the drum who’d been in the water at Jory’s to please his wife, and he came up humming, and there’s not a mark on his paper. It’s something the six of them have, and you have, and the rest of the river hasn’t. They tell me what they think it is. I can only tell you where it shows. I can’t tell you it lives there. A fire shows in the chimney.”

He looked at Sol over the glasses. “That’s a theory, Tarren, not a sermon. If there were a journal left in the worlds, I’d send it in, and some cleverer man would tell me where I’d gone wrong. There isn’t. So it lives in a drawer. I’d like to watch it: the aging, and this. Once a week, if you’ll let me.”
“Why?”
Lucan considered it, as if it were a fair question.

“Because I’ve spent thirty-one years on the far side of the church’s machines, writing down what they can’t see, in the margins of other things. And now there’s a man in my surgery who has been on both ends of the custody form. Who signed for them, and then fell down and became one, and can tell me what it’s like from the inside.” He took down a ledger bound in grey board, new, its pages blank. “I’d like to do it properly. From the beginning.”
He opened it on the table and uncapped his pen, and at the top of the first page he wrote the date, and under it: Sol Tarren.
It was evening before Sol left. Lucan brought out bread and two cups of something the chandler made from reed, and they ate at the end of the long table.
“You don’t believe any of it,” Sol said. “The church.”

“I don’t believe things. I count them.” Lucan turned his cup a quarter turn. “You were a bishop for centuries. Would you like the arguments against? I’ve never had anyone to try them on who’d know if they were any good.”
He did not wait for an answer. He had, Sol saw, been saving them a long time. He counted them off on his long fingers with something that in another man would have been glee.

“One. They call it the Virus. A virus passes. I’ve never once seen this pass from one person to another, not husband to wife, not mother to the child at her breast. You could seize in the middle of the Bounty Market and bleed on a thousand people, and not one of them would catch it. Four hundred years, and nobody’s checked. Whoever named it wasn’t describing it. A name like that is a fence. It’s there so nobody will stand close enough to hear what they say afterward.

“Two. Renewal takes out grief, and they call that mercy. Grief is a sound mind closing a wound. If a man came up my stair unable to grieve for his own son, I’d go looking for the injury. The chapel calls it a sacrament, and the river comes down the steps smiling.

“Three. Heaven needs a backup. A paradise you have to be copied into, that can fail to take the copy, and keeps a holding light for the ones it drops. Heaven on this river comes in through a grey cabinet in my cellar, and when the damp gets in, I send for parts.”
He held up the fourth finger and looked at it, as if it were the one he liked best.

“Four. Mercy. The infected are released, and they rest in the City and heal, and the family gets a resting light in the Pearl. I’ve sat with those families. Thirty-one years, Tarren, and I’ve never met one that had a visit from anyone in Mercy. Not a word. Not a face. The failures get a holding light. The released get a resting light. Your church has a light for everyone it can’t show you.” He picked up his cup. “I’d want a long look at a hospital where nobody has ever been discharged. Is that unfair to the church, Bishop? You’d know.”
“No,” Sol said.
Lucan’s cup stopped a moment on its way up. Then it went on.

Sol sat with his hands round his own cup. He had known since the packet. He had seen them in the light, the ones he had signed for, Stephen at the end of the line, standing outside a gate that did not open. It had taken a seizure and his friend’s death to show him. This man had needed a pencil.

And it was so plain. That was the worst of it. Nothing had been hidden. Sol had carried every figure in the corner of his eye for four hundred years. He had even noticed the visits, once, and found an explanation before the thought was finished. It had needed nothing at all to keep it hidden, only that nobody count.
“Don’t take any comfort in it,” Lucan said. “I’m not on your side either. When I’ve enough cases, I’ll do your voice in the light the same way, and you won’t enjoy it.”
“No,” Sol said. “I don’t expect I will.”
That night, for the first time since Concord, Sol opened his case.

The rain had stopped. The round window over the river held a few smeared stars and the dark. He set the lamp on the floor beside the cot and took out the two books. He did not open the old one. He held it a moment, soft and loose and smelling of dust and dried flowers, and set it beside him. Then he opened Stephen’s.
The first line on the first page, in small dense slanting handwriting, was: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

His heart turned over. Then he read on, and it was not the same. The earth was without form and empty, and darkness was over the face of the deep. It was a beginning, but another one: darkness, and water, and God speaking over the water, Let there be light, and light. It was strange and enormous and plain, and there was no Word in it.
Read the one about the Word first.

He turned the pages carefully. Here and there the writing stopped in the middle of a page and there was a white space, a few lines, once nearly a whole page, and in it, in pencil, very small, Stephen had written gone, and then gone on below. Sol touched one of those white spaces with his fingertip. It was the most honest thing he had ever seen on a page.

In the end he did not find it by looking. He closed the book on his knees and let it fall open, and it fell open near the back, where the paper was softer and greyer than the rest and the spine had cracked white from being opened there over and over again.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not anything made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
He stopped.

In the beginning was Life, and Life was the light of all people. He had sung it over every cradle. The wardens sang it in the Mercy rooms, holding the hands of the dying. And here was the line it had been cut from. Someone had taken this sentence and lifted the him out of it, carefully, the way you would lift a stone out of a ring, so that the life in it belonged to no one at all, and so could belong to anyone who claimed it. He had sung the empty setting for four hundred years and called it the jewel.
And the Word was a him. All things were made through him. In him was life. It was not a thing that was said. It was someone.

The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. A man with a name, sent, the way a dockworker had been sent up a long straight street to a bishop’s door. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him.
Sol put the book down on his knees.

Received into Mercy. He had written it thousands of times, over people nobody had ever received. The ascension clerks wrote Received under every soul that went up, and when an upload failed the console wrote Not received, and the family saw the holding light. It was the church’s word. It was his word. He had never once wondered where it came from.
It was a long time before he picked the book up again.

But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God, who were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

He looked at his own hand, holding the page down in the lamplight. Renewed and renewed, and kept at forty for four centuries like a coat kept in a cupboard. Now it was flesh, the ordinary kind, the kind that went grey and folded at the knuckles and wore out. And the one through whom all things were made had chosen that. Not the hood, not the bright unchanging City. This.
The next page was there under his thumb, and the whole thick soft weight of the book after it, everything Stephen had copied by lamplight in hiding for nine years, waiting.
He did not turn it.

He was afraid of it, the way a man is afraid of a door he has been knocking on for a long time, when at last he hears footsteps coming to open it. He closed the notebook and held it against his chest, as he had held it blind in Concord, and lay back and put out the lamp.

The river went by beneath him in the dark. Somewhere in the night, without meaning to, he said the first line aloud to the empty loft, slowly, the way the old man had said it on the floor of the market, as if he were remembering it.
